Animators at SCAD Panel Emphasize Human Creativity and Defend Demanding Production Processes Against AI Shortcuts

Leading figures in the animation industry gathered in Savannah, Georgia, to discuss the future of their craft, emphasizing that the immense time and labor required to handcraft animated films are fundamental to how stories resonate with audiences. The discussion took place during Variety's "Pixels and Pencils" panel, moderated by Clayton Davis in partnership with the SCAD Savannah Film Festival.

The Demands of Handcrafted Storytelling

Panelists explored the meticulous work required to build animated worlds from the ground up. Daniel Chong of Pixar ("Hoppers") noted that every set, character, and element of cloth, hair, and atmosphere must be completely fabricated rather than captured by pointing a camera. This exhaustive process often spans years or even decades; Brad Bird shared that his upcoming Netflix project, "Ray Gunn," took roughly 30 years to finalize from its initial conception, though work on it was not continuous.

Similarly, Travis Knight discussed the grueling nature of stop-motion production for Laika's "Wildwood," which utilized 2,800 individual shots. Knight described stop-motion as a progressive medium where artists work frame by frame in slow motion to construct a performance, calling the hands-on process "extraordinarily magical."

Pushing Back Against Artificial Intelligence

As artificial intelligence continues to advance, the panelists addressed growing industry questions about technology's role in filmmaking. The group voiced strong skepticism regarding automated shortcuts that claim to generate content with the click of a button. Chong argued that the difficulty and deliberate pacing of traditional animation are precisely what make the final films great and capable of connecting with human viewers on a deep level.

Bird encouraged artists in the audience to thoroughly learn the foundational mechanics of animation as the technological landscape continues to shift. The filmmakers agreed that authentic storytelling must stem from human experience, maintaining that automated tools cannot replicate the illusion of life created by human artists.

Narrative Style and Collaboration

Beyond production techniques, the panel examined how visual styles serve individual narratives. Januel Mercado and Joel Crawford of DreamWorks Animation discussed their work on "Forgotten Island," explaining that the film's animation style shifts to reflect different characters' perspectives and memories, drawing on various anime and manga influences.

Leah Nelson, director for Independent Film Company's "Tangles," also addressed misconceptions about the medium, noting that directors do not always need to be traditional animators. Nelson shared that she communicated her vision to her team by utilizing alternative methods, such as filming live-action reference footage of herself performing actions when she could not draw them.

Practical Implications and Verification

For readers and aspiring filmmakers looking to understand the current state of animation, this panel highlights the ongoing tension between technological automation and traditional artistic labor.

  • What is confirmed: The panel featured six prominent directors and creators—Brad Bird, Daniel Chong, Joel Crawford, Januel Mercado, Travis Knight, and Leah Nelson—speaking at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival event hosted by Variety on Monday.
  • What remains unknown: The long-term impact of artificial intelligence tools on studio pipelines and commercial animation workflows has not yet been determined as the technology evolves.
  • How to verify: Readers can review the original coverage and full report of the event through the official [Variety Report](https://variety.com/2026/film/news/pixels-and-pencils-panelists-2026-1236933652/).
